entries.befda136be16aa11168f52a9d5230a6ca7ac271f: <div sID="gen3618" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="15" osisID="Deut.15" sID="Deut.15"/> <div eID="gen3618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3619" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen3620" type="x-p"/> In this chapter Moses gives orders, I. Concerning the release of debts, every seventh year (<reference osisRef="Deut.15.1-Deut.15.6">ver. 1-6</reference>), with a caution that this should be no hindrance to charitable lending, <reference osisRef="Deut.15.7-Deut.15.11">ver. 7-11</reference>. II. Concerning the release of servants after seven years' service, <reference osisRef="Deut.15.12-Deut.15.18">ver. 12-18</reference>. III. Concerning the sanctification of the firstlings of cattle to God, <reference osisRef="Deut.15.19-Deut.15.23">ver. 19</reference>, &c.
entries.dd20d402b66722d47729f655816d3bd0d7ca93f6: <div eID="gen3620" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen3619" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Year of Release. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1451.)</title> <div sID="gen3621" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> At the end of <hi type="italic">every</hi> seven years thou shalt make a release. <hi type="super">2</hi> And this <hi type="italic">is</hi> the manner of the release: Every creditor that lendeth <hi type="italic">ought</hi> unto his neighbour shall release <hi type="italic">it;</hi> he shall not exact <hi type="italic">it</hi> of his neighbour, or of his brother; because it is called the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's release. <hi type="super">3</hi> Of a foreigner thou mayest exact <hi type="italic">it again:</hi> but <hi type="italic">that</hi> which is thine with thy brother thine hand shall release; <hi type="super">4</hi> Save when there shall be no poor among you; for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall greatly bless thee in the land which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God giveth thee <hi type="italic">for</hi> an inheritance to possess it: <hi type="super">5</hi> Only if thou carefully hearken unto the voice of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God, to observe to do all these commandments which I command thee this day. <hi type="super">6</hi> For the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God blesseth thee, as he promised thee: and thou shalt lend unto many nations, but thou shalt not borrow; and thou shalt reign over many nations, but they shall not reign over thee. <hi type="super">7</hi> If there be among you a poor man of one of thy brethren within any of thy gates in thy land which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God giveth thee, thou shalt not harden thine heart, nor shut thine hand from thy poor brother: 8 But thou shalt open thine hand wide unto him, and shalt surely lend him sufficient for his need, <hi type="italic">in that</hi> which he wanteth. <hi type="super">9</hi> Beware that there be not a thought in thy wicked heart, saying, The seventh year, the year of release, is at hand; and thine eye be evil against thy poor brother, and thou givest him nought; and he cry unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> against thee, and it be sin unto thee. <hi type="super">10</hi> Thou shalt surely give him, and thine heart shall not be grieved when thou givest unto him: because that for this thing the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God shall bless thee in all thy works, and in all that thou puttest thine hand unto. <hi type="super">11</hi> For the poor shall never cease out of the land: therefore I command thee, saying, Thou shalt open thine hand wide unto thy brother, to thy poor, and to thy needy, in thy land. <div eID="gen3621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3622" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A law for the relief of poor debtors, such (we may suppose) as were insolvent. Every seventh year was a year of release, in which the ground rested from being tilled and servants were discharged from their services; and, among other acts of grace, this was one, that those who had borrowed money, and had not been able to pay it before, should this year be released from it; and though, if they were able, they were afterwards bound in conscience to repay it, yet thenceforth the creditor should never recover it by law. Many good expositors think it only forbids the exacting of the debt in the year of release, because, no harvest being gathered in that year, it could not be expected that men should pay their debts then, but that afterwards it might be sued for and recovered: so that the release did not extinguish the debt, but only stayed the process for a time. But others think it was a release of the debt for ever, and this seems more probable, yet under certain limitations expressed or implied. It is supposed (<reference osisRef="Deut.15.3">v. 3</reference>) that the debtor was an Israelite (an alien could not take the benefit of this law) and that he was poor (<reference osisRef="Deut.15.4">v. 4</reference>), that he did not borrow for trade or purchase, but for the subsistence of his family, and that now he could not pay it without reducing himself to poverty and coming under a necessity of seeking relief in other countries, which might be his temptation to revolt from God. The law is not that the creditor shall not receive the debt if the debtor, or his friends for him, can pay it; but he shall not exact it by a legal process. The reasons of this law are, 1. To put an honour upon the sabbatical year: <hi type="italic">Because it is called the Lord's release,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.15.2">v. 2</reference>. That was God's year for their land, as the weekly sabbath was God's day for themselves, their servants, and cattle; and, as by the resting of their ground, so by the release of their debts, God would teach them to depend upon his providence. This year of release typified the grace of the gospel, in which is proclaimed the acceptable year of the Lord, and by which we obtain the release of our debts, that is, the pardon of our sins, and we are taught to forgive injuries, as we are and hope to be forgiven of God. 2. It was to prevent the falling of any Israelite into extreme poverty: so the margin reads (<reference osisRef="Deut.15.4">v. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">To the end there shall be no poor among you,</hi> none miserably and scandalously poor, to the reproach of their nation and religion, the reputation of which they ought to preserve. 3. God's security is here given by a divine promise that, whatever they lost by their poor debtors, it should be made up to them in the blessing of God upon all they had and did, <reference osisRef="Deut.15.4-Deut.15.6">v. 4-6</reference>. Let them take care to do their duty, and then God would bless them with such great increase that what they might lose by bad debts, if they generously remitted them, should not be missed out of their stock at the year's end. Not only, <hi type="italic">the Lord shall bless thee</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.15.4">v. 4</reference>), but he <hi type="italic">doth bless thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.15.6">v. 6</reference>. It is altogether inexcusable if, though God had given us abundance, so that we have not only enough but to spare, yet we are rigorous and server in our demands from our poor brethren; for our abundance should be the supply of their wants, that at least there may not be such an inequality as is between two extremes, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.14">2 Cor. viii. 14</reference>. They must also consider that their land was God's gift to them, that all their increase was the fruit of God's blessing upon them, and therefore they were bound in duty to him to use and dispose of their estates as he should order and direct them. And, <hi type="italic">lastly,</hi> If they would remit what little sums they had lent to their poor brethren, it is promised that they should be able to lend great sums to their rich neighbours, <hi type="italic">even to many nations</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.15.6">v. 6</reference>), and should be enriched by those loans. Thus the nations should become subject to them, and dependent on them, as <hi type="italic">the borrower is servant to the lender,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.22.7">Prov. xxii. 7</reference>. To be able to lend, and not to have need to borrow, we must look upon as a great mercy, and a good reason why we should do good with what we have, lest we provoke God to turn the scales. <div eID="gen3622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3623" type="x-p"/> II. Here is a law in favour of poor borrowers, that they might not suffer damage by the former law. Men would be apt to argue, <hi type="italic">If the case of a man be so with his debtor</hi> that if the debt be not paid before the year of release it shall be lost, it were better not to lend. "No," says this branch of the statute, "thou shalt not think such a thought." 1. It is taken for granted that there would be poor among them, who would have occasion to borrow (<reference osisRef="Deut.15.7">v. 7</reference>), and that there would never cease to be some such objects of charity (<reference osisRef="Deut.15.7">v. 7</reference>), and that there would never cease to be some such objects of charity (<reference osisRef="Deut.15.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">The poor shall never cease out of thy land,</hi> though not such as were reduced to extreme poverty, yet such as would be behind-hand, and would have occasion to borrow; of such poor he here speaks, and such we have always with us, so that a charitable disposition may soon find a charitable occasion. 2. In such a case we are here commanded to lend or give, according to our ability and the necessity of the case: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt not harden thy heart, nor shut thy hand,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.15.7">v. 7</reference>. If the hand be shut, it is a sign the heart is hardened; for, <hi type="italic">if the clouds were full of rain, they would empty themselves,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.3">Eccl. xi. 3</reference>. Bowels of compassion would produce liberal distributions, <reference osisRef="Jas.2.15-Jas.2.16">Jam. ii. 15, 16</reference>. Thou shalt not only stretch out thy hand to him to reach him something, but thou shalt <hi type="italic">open thy hand wide unto him,</hi> to <hi type="italic">lend him sufficient,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.15.8">v. 8</reference>. Sometimes there is as much charity in prudent lending as in giving, as it obliges the borrower to industry and honesty and may put him into a way of helping himself. We are sometimes tempted to think, when an object of charity presents itself, we may choose whether we will give any thing or nothing, little or much; whereas it is here an express precept (<reference osisRef="Deut.15.11">v. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">I command thee,</hi> not only to give, but to <hi type="italic">open thy hand wide,</hi> to give liberally. 3. Here is a caveat against that objection which might arise against charitable lending from the foregoing law for the release of debts (<reference osisRef="Deut.15.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">Beware that there be not a thought,</hi> a covetous ill-natured thought, <hi type="italic">in thy Belial heart, "The year of release is at hand,</hi> and therefore I will not lend what I must then be sure to lose;" lest thy poor brother, whom thou refusest to lend to, complain to God, and it will be a sin, a great sin, to thee. Note, (1.) The law is spiritual and lays a restraint upon the thoughts of the heart. We mistake if we think thoughts are free from the divine cognizance and check. (2.) That is a wicked heart indeed that raises evil thoughts from the good law of God, as theirs did who, because God had obliged them to the charity of forgiving, denied the charity of giving. (3.) We must carefully watch against all those secret suggestions which would divert us from our duty or discourage us in it. Those that would keep from the act of sin must keep out of their minds the very thought of sin. (4.) When we have an occasion of charitable lending, if we cannot trust the borrower, we must trust God, and lend, hoping for nothing again in this world, but expecting it will be recompensed in the resurrection of the just, <reference osisRef="Luke.6.35">Luke vi. 35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.14.14">xiv. 14</reference>. (5.) It is a dreadful thing to have the cry of the poor against us, for God has his ear open to that cry, and, in compassion to them, will be sue to reckon with those that deal hardly with them. (6.) That which we think is our prudence often proves sin to us; he that refused to lend because the year of release was at hand thought he did wisely, and that men would <hi type="italic">praise him as doing well for himself,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.49.18">Ps. xlix. 18</reference>. But he is here told that he did wickedly, and that God would condemn him as doing ill to his brother; and we are sure that the <hi type="italic">judgment of God is according to truth,</hi> and that what he says is sin to us will certainly be ruin to us if it be not repented of. <div eID="gen3623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3624" type="x-p"/> III. Here is a command to give cheerfully whatever we give in charity: "<hi type="italic">Thy heart shall not be grieved when thou givest,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.15.10">v. 10</reference>. Be not loth to part with thy money on so good an account, nor think it lost; grudge not a kindness to they brother; and distrust not the providence of God, as if thou shouldest want that thyself which thou givest in charity; but, on the contrary, let it be a pleasure and a satisfaction of soul to thee to think that thou art honouring God with thy substance, doing good, making thy brother easy, and laying up for thyself a good security for the time to come. What thou doest do freely, for God <hi type="italic">loves a cheerful giver,</hi>" <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.7">2 Cor. ix. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen3624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3625" type="x-p"/> IV. Here is a promise of a recompence in this life: "<hi type="italic">For this thing the Lord thy God shall bless thee.</hi>" Covetous people say "Giving undoes us;" no, giving cheerfully in charity will enrich us, it will <hi type="italic">fill the barns with plenty</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.10">Prov. iii. 10</reference>) and the soul with true comfort, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.10-Isa.58.11">Isa. lviii. 10, 11</reference>.
entries.0c4eeb649c4259b51e393d1a92148162a44816cc: <div eID="gen3625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3626" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super"></hi> 12 <hi type="italic">And</hi> if thy brother, a Hebrew man, or a Hebrew woman, be sold unto thee, and serve thee six years; then in the seventh year thou shalt let him go free from thee. <hi type="super">13</hi> And when thou sendest him out free from thee, thou shalt not let him go away empty: <hi type="super">14</hi> Thou shalt furnish him liberally out of thy flock, and out of thy floor, and out of thy winepress: <hi type="italic">of that</hi> wherewith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God hath blessed thee thou shalt give unto him. <hi type="super">15</hi> And thou shalt remember that thou wast a bondman in the land of Egypt, and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God redeemed thee: therefore I command thee this thing to day. <hi type="super">16</hi> And it shall be, if he say unto thee, I will not go away from thee; because he loveth thee and thine house, because he is well with thee; <hi type="super">17</hi> Then thou shalt take an awl, and thrust <hi type="italic">it</hi> through his ear unto the door, and he shall be thy servant for ever. And also unto thy maidservant thou shalt do likewise. <hi type="super">18</hi> It shall not seem hard unto thee, when thou sendest him away free from thee; for he hath been worth a double hired servant <hi type="italic">to thee,</hi> in serving thee six years: and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God shall bless thee in all that thou doest. <div eID="gen3626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3627" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A repetition of the law that had been given concerning Hebrew servants who had sold themselves for servants, or were sold by their parents through extreme poverty, or were sold by the court of judgment for some crime committed. The law was, 1. That they should serve but six years, and in the seventh should go out free, <reference osisRef="Deut.15.12">v. 12</reference>. Compare <reference osisRef="Exod.21.2">Exod. xxi. 2</reference>. And, if the year of jubilee happened before they served out their time, that would be their discharge. God's Israel were a free people, and must not be compelled to perpetual slavery; thus are God's spiritual Israel called unto liberty. 2. That if, when their six years' service had expired, they had no mind to go out free, but would rather continue in service, as having less care, though taking more pains, than their masters, in this case they must lay themselves under an obligation to serve for ever, that is, for life, by having <hi type="italic">their ears bored to the door-posts,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.15.16-Deut.15.17">v. 16, 17</reference>. Compare <reference osisRef="Exod.21.6">Exod. xxi. 6</reference>. If hereby a man disgraced himself with some, as of a mean and servile spirit, that had not a due sense of the honour and pleasure of liberty, yet, we may suppose, with others he got reputation, as of a quiet contented spirit, humble, and diligent, and loving, and not <hi type="italic">given to change.</hi> <div eID="gen3627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3628" type="x-p"/> II. Here is an addition to this law, requiring them to put some small stock into their servants' hands to set up with for themselves, when they sent them out of their service, <reference osisRef="Deut.15.13-Deut.15.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. It was to be supposed that they had nothing of their own, and that their friends had little or nothing for them, else they else they would have been redeemed before they were discharged by law; they had no wages for their service, and all they got by their labour was their masters', so that their liberty would do them little good, having nothing to begin the world with; therefore their masters are here commanded to furnish them liberally with corn and cattle. No certain measure is prescribed: that is left to the generosity of the master, who probably would have respect to the servant's merit and necessity; but the Jewish writers say, "He could not give less than the value of thirty shekels of silver, but as much more as he pleased" The maid-servants, though they were not to have their ears bored if they were disposed to stay, yet, if they went out free, they were to have a gratuity given them; for to this those words refer, <hi type="italic">Unto thy maid-servant thou shalt do likewise,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.15.17">v. 17</reference>. The reasons for this are taken from the law of gratitude. They must do it, 1. In gratitude to God, who had not only brought them out of Egypt (<reference osisRef="Deut.15.15">v. 15</reference>), but brought them out greatly enriched with the spoils of the Egyptians. Let them not send their servants out empty, for they were not sent empty out of the house of bondage. God's tender care of us and kindness to us oblige us to be careful of, and kind to, those that have a dependence upon us. Thus we must <hi type="italic">render according to the benefit done unto us.</hi> 2. In gratitude to their servants, <reference osisRef="Deut.15.18">v. 18</reference>. "Grudge not to give him a little out of thy abundance, for <hi type="italic">he has been worth a double hired servant unto thee.</hi> The days of the hireling at most were but three years (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.14">Isa. xvi. 14</reference>), but he has served thee six years, and, unlike the hired servant, without any wages." Masters and landlords ought to consider what need they have of, and what ease and advantage they have by, their servants and tenants, and should not only be just but kind to them. To these reasons it is added, as before in this chapter (<reference osisRef="Deut.15.4">v. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.15.6">6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.15.10">10</reference>), <hi type="italic">The Lord thy God shall bless thee.</hi> Then we may expect family blessings, the springs of family-prosperity, when we make conscience of our duty to our family-relations.
entries.70d82795c7b4438ef878075ef345edec20052756: <div eID="gen3628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3629" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> All the firstling males that come of thy herd and of thy flock thou shalt sanctify unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God: thou shalt do no work with the firstling of thy bullock, nor shear the firstling of thy sheep. 20 Thou shalt eat <hi type="italic">it</hi> before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God year by year in the place which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall choose, thou and thy household. <hi type="super">21</hi> And if there be <hi type="italic">any</hi> blemish therein, <hi type="italic">as if it be</hi> lame, or blind, <hi type="italic">or have</hi> any ill blemish, thou shalt not sacrifice it unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God. <hi type="super">22</hi> Thou shalt eat it within thy gates: the unclean and the clean <hi type="italic">person shall eat it</hi> alike, as the roebuck, and as the hart. <hi type="super">23</hi> Only thou shalt not eat the blood thereof; thou shalt pour it upon the ground as water. <div eID="gen3629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3630" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. A repetition of the law concerning the firstlings of their cattle, that, if they were males, they were to be <hi type="italic">sanctified to the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.15.19">v. 19</reference>), in remembrance of, and in thankfulness for, the sparing of the first-born of Israel, when the first-born of the Egyptians, both of man and beast, were slain by the destroying angel (<reference osisRef="Exod.13.2">Exod. xiii. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.13.15">15</reference>); on the eighth day it was to be given to God ( <reference osisRef="Exod.22.30">Exod. xxii. 30</reference>), and to be divided between the priest and the altar, <reference osisRef="Num.18.17-Num.18.18">Num. xviii. 17, 18</reference>. 2. An addition to that law, for the further explication of it, directing them what to do with the firstlings, (1.) That were females: "Thou shalt <hi type="italic">do no work with the</hi> female <hi type="italic">firstlings of the cow,</hi> nor shear those of the sheep" (<reference osisRef="Deut.15.19">v. 19</reference>); of them the learned bishop Patrick understands it. Though the female firstlings were not so entirely sanctified to God as the males, nor so early as at eight days old, yet they were not to be converted by the owners to their own use as the other cattle, but must be offered to God as peace-offerings, or used in a religious feast, at the year's end, <reference osisRef="Deut.15.20">v. 20</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thou shalt eat it before the Lord thy God,</hi> as directed <reference osisRef="Deut.12.18">ch. xii. 18</reference>. (2.) But what must they do with that which was blemished, ill-blemished? <reference osisRef="Deut.15.21">v. 21</reference>. Were it male or female, it must not be brought near the sanctuary, nor used either for sacrifice or for holy feasting, for it would not be fit to honour God with, nor to typify Christ, who is a <hi type="italic">Lamb without blemish;</hi> yet it must not be reared, but killed and eaten at their own houses as common food (<reference osisRef="Deut.15.22">v. 22</reference>), only they must be sure <hi type="italic">not to eat it with the blood,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.15.23">v. 23</reference>. The frequent repetition of this caution intimates what need the people had of it, and what stress God laid upon it. What a mercy it is that we are not under this yoke! We are not dieted as they were; we make no difference between a first calf, or lamb, and the rest that follow. Let us therefore realize the gospel meaning of this law, devoting ourselves and the first of our time and strength to God, as a kind of first-fruits of his creatures, and using all our comforts and enjoyments to his praise and under the direction of his law, as we have them all by his gift.  <chapter eID="Deut.15"/> <div eID="gen3630" type="x-p"/>

entries.e6cef00967eb69df6488c1b7e5d4e8388380969a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1782"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 15</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Deut.15.1-Deut.15.11">De 15:1-11</reference>. The Seventh Year, a Year of Release for the Poor.</title> <div sID="gen2388" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1782"/><hi type="bold">1. At the end of every seven years--</hi>during the last of the seven, that is, the sabbatical year (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.2">Ex 21:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.23.11">23:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.25.4">Le 25:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.34.14">Jr 34:14</reference>). <div eID="gen2388" type="x-p"/>
entries.e9bdc5ab1e20ba14b1f091875d5aa2db6697c404: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1783"/><div sID="gen2389" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1783"/><hi type="bold">2. Every creditor that lendeth ought unto his neighbour shall release it--</hi>not by an absolute discharge of the debt, but by passing over that year without exacting payment. The relief was temporary and peculiar to that year during which there was a total suspension of agricultural labor.<div eID="gen2389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2390" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he shall not exact it ... of his brother--</hi>that is, an Israelite, so called in opposition to a stranger or foreigner.<div eID="gen2390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2391" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because it is called the Lord's release--</hi>The reason for acquitting a debtor at that particular period proceeded from obedience to the command, and a regard for the honor, of God; an acknowledgment of holding their property of Him, and gratitude for His kindness. <div eID="gen2391" type="x-p"/>
entries.5d58873070afbb3ea18334428510c959fd59a8b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1784"/><div sID="gen2392" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1784"/><hi type="bold">3. Of a foreigner thou mayest exact it again--</hi>Admission to all the religious privileges of the Israelites was freely granted to heathen proselytes, though this spiritual incorporation did not always imply an equal participation of civil rights and privileges (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.44">Le 25:44</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.34.14">Jr 34:14</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.2">1Ch 22:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.2.17">2Ch 2:17</reference>). <div eID="gen2392" type="x-p"/>
entries.f92edb80439065365573500d82c36c6f2e38f08f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1785"/><div sID="gen2393" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1785"/><hi type="bold">4. Save when there shall be no poor man among you--</hi>Apparently a qualifying clause added to limit the application of the foregoing statement [De 15:3]; so that "the brother" to be released pointed to a poor borrower, whereas it is implied that if he were rich, the restoration of the loan might be demanded even during that year. But the words may properly be rendered (as on the Margin) to the end, in order that there may be no poor among you--that is, that none be reduced to inconvenient straits and poverty by unseasonable exaction of debts at a time when there was no labor and no produce, and that all may enjoy comfort and prosperity, which will be the case through the special blessing of God on the land, provided they are obedient. <div eID="gen2393" type="x-p"/>
entries.85c0ad390f07665e6fff0a8e611dd5463b41542d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1786"/><div sID="gen2394" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1786"/><hi type="bold">7-11. If there be among you a poor man ... thou shalt not harden thine heart--</hi>Lest the foregoing law should prevent the Israelites lending to the poor, Moses here admonishes them against so mean and selfish a spirit and exhorts them to give in a liberal spirit of charity and kindness, which will secure the divine blessing (<reference osisRef="Rom.12.8">Ro 12:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.7">2Co 9:7</reference>). <div eID="gen2394" type="x-p"/>
entries.1062ef2030eaf6724a5acf4098b3cc22cadbfb88: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1788"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Deut.15.12-Deut.15.19">De 15:12-19</reference>. Hebrew Servants' Freedom.</title> <div sID="gen2396" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1788"/><hi type="bold">12. if thy brother, an Hebrew man, or an Hebrew woman, be sold unto thee--</hi>The last extremity of an insolvent debtor, when his house or land was not sufficient to cancel his debt, was to be sold as a slave with his family (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.39">Le 25:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.1">2Ki 4:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.5.1-Neh.5.13">Ne 5:1-13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.24.9">Job 24:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.18.25">Mt 18:25</reference>). The term of servitude could not last beyond six years. They obtained their freedom either after six years from the time of their sale or before the end of the seventh year. At the year of jubilee, such slaves were emancipated even if their six years of service were not completed [see on Le 25:39]. <div eID="gen2396" type="x-p"/>
entries.e751d5954fbb4836e01488bd16556df35f4a45cc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1789"/><div sID="gen2397" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1789"/><hi type="bold">13-15. thou shalt not let him go away empty--</hi>A seasonable and wise provision for enabling a poor unfortunate to regain his original status in society, and the motive urged for his kindness and humanity to the Hebrew slave was the remembrance that the whole nation was once a degraded and persecuted band of helots in Egypt. Thus, kindness towards their slaves, unparalleled elsewhere in those days, was inculcated by the Mosaic law; and in all their conduct towards persons in that reduced condition, leniency and gentleness were enforced by an appeal which no Israelite could resist. <div eID="gen2397" type="x-p"/>
entries.a4731022c390ee7945c947ef9f3b2197c31a7a27: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1790"/><div sID="gen2398" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1790"/><hi type="bold">16-17. if he say unto thee, I will not go away from thee--</hi>If they declined to avail themselves of the privilege of release and chose to remain with their master, then by a peculiar form of ceremony they became a party to the transaction, voluntarily sold themselves to their employer, and continued in his service till death. <div eID="gen2398" type="x-p"/>
entries.b18dfd2520ef12e93c6680c24ee1eb995c4f283f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1791"/><div sID="gen2399" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1791"/><hi type="bold">18. he hath been worth a double hired servant to thee--</hi>that is, he is entitled to double wages because his service was more advantageous to you, being both without wages and for a length of time, whereas hired servants were engaged yearly (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.53">Le 25:53</reference>), or at most for three years (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.14">Is 16:14</reference>). <div eID="gen2399" type="x-p"/>
entries.6617cdfd849a68deda04df3a5c5ea42ad9458ab0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1792"/><div sID="gen2400" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1792"/><hi type="bold">19. All the firstling males of thy herd and of thy flock thou shalt sanctify unto the Lord thy God--</hi>[See on Ex 13:2]; see <reference osisRef="Exod.22.30">Ex 22:30</reference>).<div eID="gen2400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2401" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou shalt do not work with the firstling of thy bullock--</hi>that is, the second firstlings (see <reference osisRef="Deut.12.17">De 12:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.12.18">18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.14.23">14:23</reference>). <chapter eID="Deut.15"/>

entries.f0cae10699cf825eb870823e189d6f98f55d3b74: <div eID="gen6732" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen6733" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6734" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6734" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6733" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6735" type="x-p"/> The Sabbatical year of release, <reference osisRef="Deu.15.1">Deu 15:1</reference>. The manner in which this release shall take place, <reference osisRef="Deu.15.2-Deu.15.5">Deu 15:2-5</reference>. Of lending to the poor, and the disposition in which it should be done, <reference osisRef="Deu.15.6-Deu.15.11">Deu 15:6-11</reference>. Of the Hebrew servant who has served six years, and who shall be dismissed well furnished, <reference osisRef="Deu.15.12-Deu.15.15">Deu 15:12-15</reference>. The ceremony of boring the ear, when the servant wishes to continue with his master, <reference osisRef="Deu.15.16-Deu.15.18">Deu 15:16-18</reference>. Of the firstlings of the flock and herd, <reference osisRef="Deu.15.19">Deu 15:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.15.20">Deu 15:20</reference>. Nothing shall be offered that has any blemish, <reference osisRef="Deu.15.21">Deu 15:21</reference>. The sacrifice to be eaten both by the clean and unclean, except the blood, which is never to be eaten, but poured out upon the ground, <reference osisRef="Deu.15.22">Deu 15:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.15.23">Deu 15:23</reference>. <div eID="gen6735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6736" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen6736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6737" type="x-p"/> At the end of every seven years thou shalt make a release - For an explanation of many things in this chapter, see the notes on Exodus 21 (note), Exodus 23 (note), and Leviticus 25 (note).
entries.82f7496797e11345b73843749ac83c1b2b1edeae: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen6737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6738" type="x-p"/> There shall be no poor - That is, comparatively; see <reference osisRef="Deu.15.11">Deu 15:11</reference>.
entries.5b1fcf9e3e074fa76c447d451f00cc1dbf340b76: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen6738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6739" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt open thine hand wide - Thy benevolence shall be in proportion to his distress and poverty, and thy ability. Thou shalt have no other rule to regulate thy charity by.
entries.281551b4b0d81fd755a4f0ea16a4507b1ff1bcef: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen6739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6740" type="x-p"/> Beware that there be not a thought in thy wicked heart - לבבך בליעל lebabecha beliyaal, thy belial heart, that is, thy good-for-nothing or unprofitable heart; See on <reference osisRef="Deu.13.13">Deu 13:13</reference> (note). <div eID="gen6740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6741" type="x-p"/> And thine eye be evil - An evil eye signifies a covetous disposition. See the same form of expression used by our Lord in the same sense, <reference osisRef="Mat.6.23">Mat 6:23</reference>. If thine eye be evil - If thou be a covetous person. Evil eye is by our Lord opposed to single eye, i. e., a person of a liberal, benevolent mind. Covetousness darkens the soul; liberality and benevolence enlighten it. <div eID="gen6741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6742" type="x-p"/> And he cry unto the Lord against thee - What a consolation to the poor and the oppressed, that they have a sure friend in God, who will hear their cry and redress their grievances!
entries.ad72b192f276845d74a53ed28ac5d737e9a3307d: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen6742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6743" type="x-p"/> For the poor shall never cease out of the land - To this passage our Lord appears to allude <reference osisRef="Mar.14.7">Mar 14:7</reference> : For ye have the poor with you always. God leaves these in mercy among men to exercise the feelings of compassion, tenderness, mercy, etc. And without occasions afforded to exercise these, man would soon become a Stoic or a brute.
entries.1339096bff01583d9109f721038e52a6b984e58d: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen6743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6744" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt not let him go away empty - Because during the time he served thee, he made no property for himself, having been always honest towards thee; and now when he leaves thee, he has nothing to begin the world with.
entries.2038239c832155a4216729f324189911107f3ceb: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen6744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6745" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt furnish him - out of thy flock - Thou shalt give him some cattle to breed with; out of thy floor - some corn for seed and for bread; and out of thy wine press - an adequate provision of wine for present necessity.
entries.7e3fbb3aa77251b6467b7174df572acd98c1ff97: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen6745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6746" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt take an awl - See the note on <reference osisRef="Exo.21.6">Exo 21:6</reference>.
entries.537178827ed22d1d94ae9823619a398f1e0aa7ce: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen6746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6747" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt eat it - in the place which the Lord shall choose - Thus God in his mercy made their duty and interest go hand in hand. And in every case God acts thus with his creatures; well, therefore, might Satan ask, Doth Job serve God for naught? No! nor does God design that any man should.
entries.ab0561332918c086932bdbebead45224655bb9c5: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen6747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6748" type="x-p"/> If there be any blemish - See the notes on <reference osisRef="Lev.22.20">Lev 22:20</reference>. God will have both a perfect priest and a perfect offering.  <chapter eID="Deut.15"/> <div eID="gen6748" type="x-p"/>

entries.2f2b54470b7cef9ae4ad1c8fc538391d4a5a7455: <reference osisRef="Deut.15.1-Deut.15.2">Deu 15:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen2325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2326" type="x-p"/> On the Year of Release. - The first two regulations in this chapter, viz., <reference osisRef="Deut.15.1-Deut.15.11">Deu 15:1-11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.15.12-Deut.15.18">Deu 15:12-18</reference>, follow simply upon the law concerning the poor tithe in <reference osisRef="Deut.14.28">Deu 14:28</reference>-29. The Israelites were not only to cause those who had no possessions (Levites, strangers, widows, and orphans) to refresh themselves with the produce of their inheritance, but they were not to force and oppress the poor. Debtors especially were not to be deprived of the blessings of the sabbatical year (<reference osisRef="Deut.15.1-Deut.15.6">Deu 15:1-6</reference>). “<hi type="italic">At the end of seven years thou shalt make a release</hi>.” The expression, “at the end of seven years,” is to be understood in the same way as the corresponding phrase, “at the end of three years,” in Deu 14:28. The end of seven years, i.e., of the seven years’ cycle formed by the sabbatical year, is mentioned as the time when debts that had been contracted were usually wiped off or demanded, after the year’s harvest had been gathered in (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.31.10">Deu 31:10</reference>, according to which the feast of Tabernacles occurred at the end of the year). שׁמטּה, from שׁמט morf ,, to let lie, to let go (cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.23.11">Exo 23:11</reference>), does not signify a remission of the debt, the relinquishing of all claim for payment, as <hi type="italic">Philo</hi> and the Talmudists affirm, but simply lengthening the term, not pressing for payment. This is the explanation in <reference osisRef="Deut.15.2">Deu 15:2</reference> : “<hi type="italic">This is the manner of the release</hi>” (<hi type="italic">shemittah</hi>): cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.19.4">Deu 19:4</reference>; 1Ki 9:15. “<hi type="italic">Every owner of a loan of his hand shall release </hi>(leave) <hi type="italic">what he has lent to his neighbour; he shall not press his neighbour, and indeed his brother; for they have proclaimed release for Jehovah</hi>.” As שׁמוט (release) points unmistakeably back to <reference osisRef="Exod.23.11">Exo 23:11</reference>, it must be interpreted in the same manner here as there. And as it is not used there to denote the entire renunciation of a field or possession, so here it cannot mean the entire renunciation of what had been lent, but simply leaving it, i.e., not pressing for it during the seventh year. This is favoured by what follows, “<hi type="italic">thou shalt not press thy neighbour</hi>,” which simply forbids an unreserved demand, but does not require that the debt should be remitted or presented to the debtor (see also Bähr, <hi type="italic">Symbolik</hi>, ii. pp. 570-1). “The loan of the hand:” what the hand has lent to another. “The master of the loan of the hand:” i.e., the owner of a loan, the lender. “His brother” defines with greater precision the idea of “a neighbour.” Calling a release, presupposes that the sabbatical year was publicly proclaimed, like the year of jubilee (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.9">Lev 25:9</reference>). קרא is impersonal (“they call”), as in <reference osisRef="Gen.11.9">Gen 11:9</reference> and Gen 16:14. “<hi type="italic">For Jehovah:</hi>” i.e., in honour of Jehovah, sanctified to Him, as in Exo 12:42. - This law points back to the institution of the sabbatical year in <reference osisRef="Exod.23.10">Exo 23:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.25.2-Lev.25.7">Lev 25:2-7</reference>, though it is not to be regarded as an appendix to the law of the sabbatical year, or an expansion of it, but simply as an exposition of what was already implied in the main provision of that law, viz., that the cultivation of the land should be suspended in the sabbatical year. If no harvest was gathered in, and even such produce as had grown without sowing was to be left to the poor and the beasts of the field, the landowner could have no income from which to pay his debts. The fact that the “<hi type="italic">sabbatical year</hi>” is not expressly mentioned, may be accounted for on the ground, that even in the principal law itself this name does not occur; and it is simply commanded that every seventh year there was to be a sabbath of rest to the land (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.4">Lev 25:4</reference>). In the subsequent passages in which it is referred to (<reference osisRef="Deut.15.9">Deu 15:9</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.31.10">Deu 31:10</reference>), it is still not called a sabbatical year, but simply the “year of release,” and that not merely with reference to debtors, but also with reference to the release (<hi type="italic">Shemittah</hi>) to be allowed to the field (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.11">Exo 23:11</reference>).
entries.201190f0098e71f36b7c964eb80c2368809de2a8: <reference osisRef="Deut.15.3">Deu 15:3</reference> <div eID="gen2326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2327" type="x-p"/> The foreigner thou mayest press, but what thou hast with thy brother shall thy hand let go. נכרי is a stranger of another nation, standing in no inward relation to Israel at all, and is to be distinguished from גּר, the foreigner who lived among the Israelites, who had a claim upon their protection and pity. This rule breathes no hatred of foreigners, but simply allows the Israelites the right of every creditor to demand his debts, and enforce the demand upon foreigners, even in the sabbatical year. There was no severity in this, because foreigners could get their ordinary income in the seventh year as well as in any other.
entries.4909ca5836a99d703ecf569b9cefe2b25ac73df8: <reference osisRef="Deut.15.4">Deu 15:4</reference> <div eID="gen2327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2328" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">Only that there shall be no poor with thee</hi>.” יהיה is jussive, like the foregoing imperfects. The meaning in this connection is, “Thou needest not to remit a debt to foreigners in the seventh year; thou hast only to take care that there is no poor man with or among thee, that thou dost not cause or increase their poverty, by oppressing the brethren who have borrowed of thee.” Understood in this way, the sentence is not at all at variance with <reference osisRef="Deut.15.11">Deu 15:11</reference>, where it is stated that the poor would never cease out of the land. The following clause, “for Jehovah will bless thee,” etc., gives a reason for the main thought, that they were not to press the Israelitish debtor. The creditor, therefore, had no need to fear that he would suffer want, if he refrained from exacting his debt from his brother in the seventh year.
entries.5e57d2357dea9b869046e79ae6d5471d1b910cc9: <reference osisRef="Deut.15.5-Deut.15.6">Deu 15:5-6</reference> <div eID="gen2328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2329" type="x-p"/> This blessing would not fail, if the Israelites would only hearken to the voice of the Lord; “<hi type="italic">for Jehovah blesseth thee</hi>” (by the perfect בּרכך, the blessing is represented not as a possible and future one only, but as one already bestowed according to the counsel of God, and, so far as the commencement was concerned, already fulfilled), “<hi type="italic">as He hath spoken</hi>” (see at <reference osisRef="Deut.1.11">Deu 1:11</reference>). “<hi type="italic">And thou wilt lend on pledge to many nations, but thou thyself wilt not borrow upon pledge</hi>.” עבט, a <hi type="italic">denom</hi>. verb, from עבוט, a pledge, signifies in <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> to give a pledge for the purpose of borrowing; in <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi>, to cause a person to give a pledge, or furnish occasion for giving a pledge, i.e., to lend upon pledge. “<hi type="italic">And thou wilt rule over many nations</hi>,” etc. Ruling is mentioned here as the result of superiority in wealth (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.28.1">Deu 28:1</reference> : <hi type="italic">Schultz</hi>).
entries.6a20a9646f128e86d768417f3ac1fbf3e4d9744b: <reference osisRef="Deut.15.7-Deut.15.8">Deu 15:7-8</reference> <div eID="gen2329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2330" type="x-p"/> And in general Israel was to be ready to lend to the poor among its brethren, not to harden its heart, to be hard-hearted, but to lend to the poor brother מחסרו דּי, “the sufficiency of his need,” whatever he might need to relieve his wants.
entries.6dad489fbf70d0ea5b2200cb5a7e295abd35012c: <reference osisRef="Deut.15.9-Deut.15.10">Deu 15:9-10</reference> <div eID="gen2330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2331" type="x-p"/> Thus they were also to beware “<hi type="italic">that there was not a word in the heart, worthlessness,</hi>” i.e., that a worthless thought did not arise in their hearts (בּליּעל is the predicate of the sentence, as the more precise definition of the word that was in the heart); so that one should say, “<hi type="italic">The seventh year is at hand, the year of release,</hi>” sc., when I shall not be able to demand what I have lent, and “<hi type="italic">that thine eye be evil towards thy poor brother,</hi>” i.e., that thou cherishest ill-will towards him (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.28.54">Deu 28:54</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.56">Deu 28:56</reference>), “<hi type="italic">and givest him not, and he appeals to Jehovah against thee, and it becomes sin to thee,</hi>” sc., which brings down upon thee the wrath of God.
entries.3af82736d18c6058f53ed122bad435fefb27312b: <reference osisRef="Deut.15.11">Deu 15:11</reference> <div eID="gen2332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2333" type="x-p"/> For the poor will never cease in the land, even the land that is richly blessed, because poverty is not only the penalty of sin, but is ordained by God for punishment and discipline.
entries.3128c2bf2bbaa7e46dc5a445765b1bdb839f5f23: <reference osisRef="Deut.15.12-Deut.15.14">Deu 15:12-14</reference> <div eID="gen2333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2334" type="x-p"/> These provisions in favour of the poor are followed very naturally by the rules which the Israelites were to be urged to observe with reference to the <hi type="italic">manumission of Hebrew slaves</hi>. It is not the reference to the sabbatical year in the foregoing precepts which forms the introduction to the laws which follow respecting the manumission of Hebrews who had become slaves, but the poverty and want which compelled Hebrew men and women to sell themselves as slaves. The seventh year, in which they were to be set free, is not the same as the sabbatical year, therefore, but the seventh year of bondage. Manumission in the seventh year of service had already been commanded in <reference osisRef="Exod.21.2-Exod.21.6">Exo 21:2-6</reference>, in the rights laid down for the nation, with special reference to the conclusion of the covenant. This command is not repeated here for the purpose of extending the law to Hebrew women, who are not expressly mentioned in Ex 21; ; for that would follow as a matter of course, in the case of a law which was quite as applicable to women as to men, and was given without any reserve to the whole congregation. It is rather repeated here as a law which already existed as a right, for the purpose of explaining the true mode of fulfilling it, viz., that it was not sufficient to give a man-servant and maid-servant their liberty after six years of service, which would not be sufficient relief to those who had been obliged to enter into slavery on account of poverty, if they had nothing with which to set up a home of their own; but love to the poor was required to do more than this, namely, to make some provision for the continued prosperity of those who were set at liberty. “<hi type="italic">If thou let him go free from thee, thou shalt not let him go</hi> (send him away) <hi type="italic">empty:</hi>” this was the new feature which Moses added here to the previous law. “<hi type="italic">Thou shalt load</hi> (העניק, lit., put upon the neck) <hi type="italic">of thy flock, and of thy floor</hi> (corn), <hi type="italic">and of thy press</hi> (oil and wine); <hi type="italic">wherewith thy God hath blessed thee, of that thou shalt give to him</hi>.”
entries.04b03db360af511842dcfd15c792cc163c7b6116: <reference osisRef="Deut.15.15">Deu 15:15</reference> <div eID="gen2334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2335" type="x-p"/> They were to be induced to do this by the recollection of their own redemption out of the bondage of Egypt, - the same motive that is urged for the laws and exhortations enjoining compassion towards foreigners, servants, maids, widows, orphans, and the poor, not only in <reference osisRef="Deut.5.15">Deu 5:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.10.19">Deu 10:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.16.12">Deu 16:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.24.18">Deu 24:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.24.22">Deu 24:22</reference>, but also in <reference osisRef="Exod.22.20">Exo 22:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.23.9">Exo 23:9</reference>, and Lev 19:34.
entries.c1f4ea30bd8cc71faa9db27fefd4bb44ca4a03ea: <reference osisRef="Deut.15.16-Deut.15.17">Deu 15:16-17</reference> <div eID="gen2335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2336" type="x-p"/> But if the man-servant and the maid-servant should not wish for liberty in the sixth year, because it was well with them in the house of their master, they were not to be compelled to go, but were to be bound to eternal, i.e., lifelong bondage, in the manner prescribed in <reference osisRef="Exod.21.5">Exo 21:5</reference>-6.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Knobel's</hi> assertion, that the judicial process enjoined in <reference osisRef="Exod.21.6">Exo 21:6</reference> does not seem to have been usual in the author’s own time, is a worthless <hi type="italic">argumentum e silentio</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen2336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2337" type="x-p"/> This is repeated from Ex 21, to guard against such an application of the law as might be really cruelty under the circumstances rather than love. Manumission was only an act of love, when the person to be set free had some hope of success and of getting a living for himself; and where there was no such prospect, compelling him to accept of freedom might be equivalent to thrusting him away.
entries.c0929bfc62a55f942b2f48322d33faab13916f01: <reference osisRef="Deut.15.18">Deu 15:18</reference> <div eID="gen2337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2338" type="x-p"/> If, on the other hand, the servant (or maid) wished to be set free, the master was not to think it hard; “<hi type="italic">for the double of the wages of a day-labourer he has earned for thee for six years</hi>,” i.e., not “twice the time of a day-labourer, so that he had really deserved twice the wages” (<hi type="italic">Vatablius, Ad. Osiander, J. Gerhard</hi>), for it cannot be proved from <reference osisRef="Isa.16.14">Isa 16:14</reference>, that a day-labourer generally hired himself out for three years; nor yet, “he has been obliged to work much harder than a day-labourer, very often by night as well as day” (<hi type="italic">Clericus, J. H. Michaelis, Rosenmüller, Baumgarten</hi>); but simply, “he has earned and produced so much, that if you had been obliged to keep a day-labourer in his place, it would have cost you twice as much” (<hi type="italic">Schultz,</hi> <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>).
entries.45cedc602d5107b2421326a49ec90cf99f4a4bc0: <reference osisRef="Deut.15.19-Deut.15.23">Deu 15:19-23</reference> <div eID="gen2338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2339" type="x-p"/> Application of the first-born of Cattle. - From the laws respecting the poor and slaves, to which the instructions concerning the tithes (<reference osisRef="Deut.14.22-Deut.14.29">Deu 14:22-29</reference>) had given occasion, Moses returns to appropriation of the first-born of the herd and flock to sacrificial meals, which he had already touched upon in <reference osisRef="Deut.12.6">Deu 12:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.12.17">Deu 12:17</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Deut.14.23">Deu 14:23</reference>, and concludes by an explanation upon this point. The command, which the Lord had given when first they came out of Egypt (<reference osisRef="Exod.13.2">Exo 13:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.13.12">Exo 13:12</reference>), that all the first-born of the herd and flock should be sanctified to Him, is repeated here by Moses, with the express injunction that they were not to work with the first-born of cattle (by yoking them to the plough or waggon), and not to shear the first-born of sheep; that is to say, they were not to use the first-born animals which were sanctified to the Lord for their own earthly purposes, but to offer them year by year as sacrifices to the Lord, and consume them in sacrificial meals. To this he adds (<reference osisRef="Deut.15.21">Deu 15:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.15.22">Deu 15:22</reference>) that further provision, that first-born animals, which were blind or lame, or had any other bad fault, were not to be offered in sacrifice to the Lord, but, like ordinary animals used for food, could be eaten in all the towns of the land. Although the first part of this law was involved in the general laws as to the kind of animal that could be offered in sacrifice (Lev 22:19.), it was by no means unimportant to point out distinctly their applicability to the first-born, and add some instructions with regard to the way in which they were to be applied. (On <reference osisRef="Deut.15.22">Deu 15:22</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.15.23">Deu 15:23</reference>, see <reference osisRef="Deut.12.15">Deu 12:15</reference> and Deu 12:16.) The annual feasts appointed by the law were to be celebrated, like the sacrificial meals, at the place which the Lord would choose for the revelation of His name; and there Israel was to rejoice before the Lord with the presentation of sacrifices. From this point of view Moses discusses the feasts of Passover, Pentecost, and Tabernacles, assuming the laws previously given concerning these festivals (Ex 12; <reference osisRef="Lev.23.1">Lev 23:1</reference>, and Num 28 and 29) as already known, and simply repeating those points which related to the sacrificial meals held at these festivals. This serves to explain the reason why only those three festivals are mentioned, at which Israel had already been commanded to appear before the Lord in <reference osisRef="Exod.23.14-Exod.23.17">Exo 23:14-17</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Exod.34.18">Exo 34:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.34.24-Exod.34.25">Exo 34:24-25</reference>, and not the feast of trumpets or day of atonement: viz., because the people were not required to assemble at the sanctuary out of the whole land on the occasion of these two festivals.<note placement="foot">That the assembling of the people at the central sanctuary is the leading point of view under which the feasts are regarded here, has been already pointed out by <hi type="italic">Bachmann</hi> (<hi type="italic">die Feste,</hi> p. 143), who has called attention to the fact that “the place which Jehovah thy God will choose” occurs six times (<reference osisRef="Deut.16.2">Deu 16:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.16.6">Deu 16:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.16.7">Deu 16:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.16.11">Deu 16:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.16.15">Deu 16:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.16.16">Deu 16:16</reference>); and “before the face of Jehovah” three times (<reference osisRef="Deut.16.11">Deu 16:11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.16.16">Deu 16:16</reference> twice); and that the celebration of the feast at any other place is expressly declared to be null and void. At the same time, he has once more thoroughly exploded the contradictions which are said to exist between this chapter and the earlier festal laws, and which <hi type="italic">Hupfeld</hi> has revived in his comments upon the feasts, without troubling himself to notice the careful discussion of the subject by <hi type="italic">Hävernick</hi> in his Introduction, and Hengstenberg in his <hi type="italic">Dissertations</hi>.</note>  <chapter eID="Deut.15"/> <div eID="gen2339" type="x-p"/>

entries.89353ca5442e1c526aede7d2a29bcf830037af49: <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.15.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Deut.15.1" sID="gen15831" type="section"/><p/> <div sID="gen15832" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> <hi type="italic">At the end of every seven years</hi>. A special act of humanity towards each other is here prescribed to the Jews, that every seven years, brother should remit to brother whatever was owed him. But, although we are not bound by this law at present, and it would not be even expedient that it should be in use, still the object to which it tended ought still to be maintained, <hi type="italic">i</hi> <hi type="italic">e</hi>., that we should not be too rigid in exacting our debts, especially if we have to do with the needy, who are bowed down by the burden of poverty. The condition of the ancient people, as I have said, was different. They derived their origin from a single race; the land of Canaan was their common inheritance; fraternal association was to be mutually sustained among them, just as if they were one family: and, inasmuch as God had once enfranchised them, the best plan for preserving’ their liberty for ever was to maintain a condition of mediocrity, lest a few persons of immense wealth should oppress the general body. Since, therefore, the rich, if they had been permitted constantly to increase in wealth, would have tyrannized over the rest, God put by this law a restraint on immoderate power. Moreover, when rest was given to the land, and men reposed from its cultivation, it was just that the whole people, for whose sake the Sabbath was instituted, should enjoy some relaxation. Still the remission here spoken of was, in my opinion, merely temporary. Some, indeed, suppose that all debts were then entirely cancelled; <note n="144"> <div sID="gen15833" type="x-p"/> “The Hebrews (says Ainsworth) for the most part hold the remission to be perpetual.” He, however, argues from the word <foreign xml:lang="he">שמטה</foreign>, <hi type="italic">an</hi> <hi type="italic">intermission</hi>, and its use in that sense in <reference osisRef="Bible:Exod.23.11">Exodus 23:11</reference>, that <hi type="italic">C</hi>.’<hi type="italic">s</hi> interpretation is the correct one. So also Dathe, who quotes Jos. Meyer in his Treatise on the Festivals of the Jews, ch. 17 sec. 20; and Michaelis, in his Laws of Moses, P. 3. sec. 157.<div eID="gen15833" type="x-p"/> </note> as if the Sabbatical year destroyed all debtor and creditor accounts; but this is refuted by the context, for when the Sabbatical year is at hand, God commands them to lend freely, whereas the contract would have been ridiculous, unless it had been lawful to seek repayment in due time. Surely, if no payment had ever followed, it would have been required simply to give: for what would the empty form of lending have availed if the money advanced was never to be returned to its owner? But God required all suits to cease for that year, so that no one should trouble his debtor: and, <hi type="italic">because</hi> in that year of freedom and immunity there was no hope of receiving back the money, God provides against the objection, and forbids them to be niggardly, although the delay might produce some <hi type="italic">inconvenience</hi>. First of all, therefore, He commands them to make a remission in the seventh year, <hi type="italic">i</hi> <hi type="italic">e</hi>., to abstain from exacting their debts, and to concede to the poor, as well as to the land, a truce, or vacation. On which ground Isaiah reproves the Jews for observing the Sabbath amiss, when they exact <note n="145"> <div sID="gen15834" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">A.</hi> <hi type="italic">V</hi>., “all your labors;” margin, “things wherewith ye grieve others; <hi type="italic">Heb</hi>., griefs;” <hi type="italic">C</hi>.’<hi type="italic">s</hi> own version, “omnes facultates vestras exigitis.”<div eID="gen15834" type="x-p"/> </note> their debts, and “fast for strife and debate.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.58.3 Bible:Isa.58.4">Isaiah 58:3, 4</reference>.) The form of remission is added, That no one should vex his neighbor in the year in which the release of God is proclaimed.<div eID="gen15832" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.15.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen15831" osisID="Deut.15.1" type="section"/>
entries.89cf5a4993b79f6caefb4bfce52a4d9087efa72d: <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.15.3" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Deut.15.3" sID="gen15835" type="section"/> <div sID="gen15836" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">3.</hi> <hi type="italic">Of a foreigner thou mayest exact it</hi>. An exception follows, that it should be lawful to sue foreigners, and to compel them to pay; and this for a very good reason, because it was by no means just that despisers of the Law should enjoy the Sabbatical benefit, especially when God had conferred the privilege on His elect people alone. What follows in the next verse, “Unless because there shall be no beggar,” interpreters twist into various senses. Some translate it, Nevertheless (<hi type="italic">veruntamen,</hi>) let there be no beggar among thee; as if it were a prohibition, that they should not suffer their poor brethren to be overwhelmed with poverty, without assisting them; and, lest they should object that, if they should be so liberal in giving, they would soon exhaust themselves, God anticipates them, and bids them rely upon his blessing. Others, however, understand it as a promise, and connect it thus, That there should be no beggar among them, if only they keep the Law, since then God would bless them. Nor would this meaning be very unsuitable. What they mean who expound it, Insomuch that there should be no beggar with thee, I know not. Let my readers, however, consider whether <note n="146"> <div sID="gen15837" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">S</hi>. <hi type="italic">M</hi>., <hi type="italic">However</hi>. <hi type="italic">A</hi>. <hi type="italic">V</hi>., <hi type="italic">Save</hi> <hi type="italic">when</hi>; or, in its margin, <hi type="italic">To</hi> <hi type="italic">the</hi> <hi type="italic">end</hi> <hi type="italic">that</hi>. <hi type="italic">S</hi>.<hi type="italic">M</hi>. refers to Jewish expositors as saying, “The meaning is, Thou shalt not fear that this law may do you an injury; for, if you be such zealous observers of my precepts, I will so bless you, and make all things needful for you to increase, that there shall be no poor man amongst you, to whom you need give what is lent. And if there be any person needing your assistance, and ye, for my sake, forgive his debt, as I have commanded, the man who doth thus shall not lose what was owed him, but shall receive from me a more abundant blessing.” The learned reader may find this expression further discussed in Noldii Concord. partic. Art., 509 of Annot and Vindic. — <hi type="italic">W</hi>.<div eID="gen15837" type="x-p"/> </note> <foreign xml:lang="he">אפס כי</foreign>, <hi type="italic">ephes</hi> <hi type="italic">ci</hi>, is not better rendered “unless because,” (<hi type="italic">nisi</hi> <hi type="italic">quod</hi>:) and then this clause would be read parenthetically, as if it were said, Whenever there shall be any poor among your brethren, an opportunity of doing them good is presented to you. Therefore the poverty of your brethren is to be relieved by you, in order that God may bless you. But, that the sentence may be clearer, I take the two words, <foreign xml:lang="he">אפס כי</foreign>, <hi type="italic">ephes</hi> <hi type="italic">ci</hi>, exclusively, as if it were, On no account let there be a beggar: or, howsoever it. may be, suffer not that by your fault there should be any beggar amongst you; for He would put an end to all vain excuses, and, as necessity arose, would have them disposed to give assistance, lest the poor should sink under the pressure of want and distress, tie does not, therefore, mean generally all poor persons, but only those in extreme indigence; such as the Prophet Amos complains are “sold for a pair of shoes.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Amos.2.6">Amos 2:6</reference>.) In order, then, that they may more cheerfully assist their distresses, He promises that His blessing shall be productive of greater abundance. And from hence Paul seems to have derived his exhortation to the Corinthians:<div eID="gen15836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15838" type="x-p"/>“He which soweth bountifully, shall reap also bountifully. God is able to make all grace abound toward you; that ye, always having all sufficiency in all things, may abound to every good work.: Now he that ministereth seed to the sower, <hi type="italic">shall</hi> both minister bread for your food, and multiply your seed sown, and increase the fruits of your righteousness, <hi type="italic">that</hi>, being enriched in every thing, <hi type="italic">you</hi> <hi type="italic">may</hi> <hi type="italic">abound</hi> unto all bountifulness.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.9.6-2Cor.9.11">2 Corinthians 9:6-11</reference>.)<div eID="gen15838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15839" type="x-p"/>In short, God would have them without carefulness, since He will abundantly recompense them with His blessing, if they have diminished their own stores by liberality to the poor.<div eID="gen15839" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.15.3" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen15835" osisID="Deut.15.3" type="section"/>
entries.bd2b6c29888974a703296e945339390d3350a888: <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.15.6" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Deut.15.6" sID="gen15840" type="section"/> <div sID="gen15841" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">6.</hi> <hi type="italic">For the Lord thy God blesseth thee</hi>. He confirms the foregoing declaration, but ascends from the particular to the general; for, after having taught that they might expect from God’s blessing much more than they have bestowed on the poor, he now recalls their attention to the Covenant itself, as much as to say, that whatever they have is derived from that original fountain of God’s grace, when He made them inheritors of the land of Canaan. God reminds them also that He then promised them abundant produce; and thus indicates that, if they were mean and niggardly, they would cause the land to be barren. When He says that they should lend to all nations, he speaks by way of amplification; and also in the next clause, that they should reign over the Gentiles; whence it follows, that if there were any in want among them, it would arise from the wickedness and depravity, of the people themselves.<div eID="gen15841" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.15.6" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen15840" osisID="Deut.15.6" type="section"/>
entries.026f17c9d0ae60909b74706bbe9969e30c9c38f9: <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.15.7" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Deut.15.7" sID="gen15842" type="section"/> <div sID="gen15843" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">7. </hi><hi type="italic">If there be among you a poor man</hi> The same word <foreign xml:lang="he">אביון</foreign>, <hi type="italic">ebyon</hi>, is used, which we have seen just above, verse 4; nor is there any contradiction when He commands them to relieve beggars, whom He had before forbidden to exist among His people; for the object of the prohibition was, that if any were reduced to beggary, they should not be cast out and forsaken. Now, however, He explains the mode of preventing this, viz., that the hands of the rich should be open to assist them. In order to incline them to compassion, he again reminds them of their common brotherhood, and sets before them, as its token and pledge, the land in which by God’s goodness they dwell together. Again, that they may be willing and prompt in their humanity, He forbids them to harden their heart, thereby signifying that avarice is always cruel. Finally, He applies this instruction to the year of release, viz., that they should straightway relieve their poor brethren towards the beginning of that year, just as if they would receive back in a few days the money which the poor man would retain to its end.<div eID="gen15843" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.15.7" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen15842" osisID="Deut.15.7" type="section"/>
entries.e2f9a2b9b52448541c46da4285ead5cb16ac56a3:
11. For the poor shall never cease out of the land. The notion
“I know that ye will not obey me with a perfect heart, and therefore my blessing shall be lessened towards you, and there shall be poor among you.” Hebrew commentators quoted in Munster and Fagius. — Poole’s Syn.
of those is far fetched who suppose that there would be always poor men among them, because they would not keep the law, and consequently the land would be barren on account of their unrighteousness. I admit that this is true; but God does not here ascribe it to their sins that there would always be some beggars among them, but only reminds them that there would never be wanting matter for their generosity, because He would prove what was in their hearts by setting the poor before them. For, (as I have observed above,) this is why the rich and poor meet together, and the Lord is maker of them all; because otherwise the duties of charity would not be observed unless they put them into exercise by assisting each other. Wherefore God, to stir up the inactivity of the rich, declares that lie prescribes nothing but what continual necessity will require.
Exodus 21
Exodus 21:1-6
1. Now these are the judgments which thou shalt set before them.
1. Haec sunt judicia quae propones eis.
2. If thou buy an Hebrew servant, six years he shall serve; and in the seventh he shall go out free for nothing.
2. Si emeris servum Hebraeum, sex annis serviet: septimo egredietur gratis.
3. If he came in by himself, he shall go out by himself; if he were married, then his wife shall go out with him.
3. Si cum corpore suo ingressus fuerit, cum corpore suo egredietur: si maritus mulieris erat, egredietur et uxor ejus cum ipso.
4. If his master have given him a wife, and she have born him sons or daughters; the wife and her children shall be her master’s, and he shall go out by himself.
4. Si herus ejus dederit ei uxorem, et pepererit ei filios, vel filias, uxor et filii ejus erunt heri sui: ipse vero egredietur cum corpore suo.
5. And if the servant shall plainly say, I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free:
5. Quod si dicendo dixerit servus, Diligo herum meum, et uxorem meam, et filios meos, non egredietur liber:
6. Then his master shall bring him unto the judges; he shall also bring him to the door, or unto the doorpost: and his master shall bore his ear through with an awl; and he shall serve him for ever.
6. Tunc adducet eum herus ejus ad judices, et applicabit eum ad ostium, vel ad postem, perforabitque herus ejus aurem ejus subula, et serviet ei in saeculum.
entries.31e61a5742a2468d25c0e0cda6ca20d7e3ade830: <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.15.13" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Deut.15.13" sID="gen15884" type="section"/><p/> <div sID="gen15885" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">13. </hi><hi type="italic">And when thou sendest him out free from thee</hi>. Here not only is the <hi type="italic">enfranchisement</hi> of slaves enjoined, but an exhortation to liberality is also added, viz., that they should not send away their slaves without their hire; for this is not a civil enactment for the purpose of extorting from the avaricious more than they were willing to give. The rule of Paul here applies:<div eID="gen15885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15886" type="x-p"/>“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, <hi type="italic">so</hi> <hi type="italic">let</hi> <hi type="italic">him</hi> <hi type="italic">give</hi>; not grudgingly or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.9.7">2 Corinthians 9:7</reference>.)<div eID="gen15886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15887" type="x-p"/>But, since the Hebrew slaves were brethren, God would not allow them to be placed in a worse condition than hirelings. That He commands them to be furnished out of the wine-press, and floor, and flock, does not mean that they were to be enriched, or that a large provision should be assigned to them, but He justly lays a constraint on the rich, whose varied abundance supplied them with the means of liberality; as if He would show them from whence they received their gratuitous gifts, which were at the same time a just compensation for the labors of their slaves.<div eID="gen15887" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.15.13" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen15884" osisID="Deut.15.13" type="section"/>
entries.2f5a622834dd2ab578dc0a9f9487cd97972ac849:
18. It shall not seem hard unto thee. I have lately observed how difficult and inconvenient to the Jews was the observance of this law; wherefore it is not without reason that God reproves their mean and niggardly pride, if they enfranchised their slaves grudgingly. And, indeed, He first urges them to obey on the score of justice, and then from the hope of remuneration. For He reminds them that for six years the slave had earned double the wages of a hireling, either because his life was more laborious, inasmuch as heavier tasks are required from slaves than from free-men, who are paid for their work; or because he had completed twice as long a period as hirelings were wont to be engaged for. For the Jewish (commentators)
“The Chaldee, Vatablus, and other more recent commentators translate it, Since he has served thee for six years for double the wages of a hireling; which the Hebrews thus explain, that the wages of a slave of six years’ standing are called double, because hirelings amongst the Hebrew’s only engaged themselves for three years, whereas the slave served for sir years; therefore he served twice as long, and earned twice as much.” — Corn. a Lapide in loco.
infer from this passage, that three years was the term prescribed for hired servants; and thus they suppose the six years were counted. But since this is a mere conjecture, I know not whether my opinion is not more suitable, that for six years their labors had been twice as profitable as would have been those of a free-man who is not under the compulsion of a slave.
Leviticus 25
Leviticus 25:39-55
39. And if thy brother that dwelleth by thee be waxen poor, and be sold unto thee; thou shalt not compel him to serve as a bond-servant:
39. Si attenuatus fuerit frater tuus apud te, ita ut vendat se tibi, non uteris opera ejus tanquam servi opera.
40. But as an hired servant, and as a sojourner, he shall be with thee, and shall serve thee unto the year of jubilee:
40. Tanquam mercenarius, tanquam colonus erit tecum: usque ad annum Jubilaei serviet tibi.
41. And then shall he depart from thee, both he and his children with him, and shall return unto his own family, and unto the possession of his fathers shall he return.
41. Egredietur autem a te ipse, et liberi ejus cum eo, ac revertetur ad familiam suam, et ad possessionem patrum suorum revertetur.
42. For they are my servants, which I brought forth out of the land of Egypt: they shall not be sold as bond-men.
42. Sunt enim servi mei quos eduxi e terra AEgypti: non vendentur venditione servili.
43. Thou shalt not rule over him with rigor, but shalt fear thy God.
43. Non dominaberis illis dure sed timebis a Deo tuo.
44. Both thy bond-men and thy bond-maids, which thou shalt have, shall be of the heathen that are round about you; of them shall ye buy bond-men and bond-maids.
44. Servus autem tuus et ancilla tua qui erunt tibi, de gentibus erunt quae sunt in circuitu vestro, ex iis emetis servum et ancillam.
45. Moreover, of the children of the strangers that do sojourn among you, of them shall ye buy, and of their families that are with you, which they begat in your land; and they shall be your possession:
45. Et etiam de filiis incolarum qui versantur apud vos, emetis: et de familia eorum qui apud vos sunt, quos procreaverunt in terra vestra: eruntque vobis in possessionem.
46. And ye shalt take them as an inheritance for your children after you, to inherit them for a possession; they shall be your bond-men for ever: but over your brethren the children of Israel, ye shall not rule one over another with rigor.
46. Et jure haereditario possidebitis eos pro filiis vestris post vos, ad possidendum possessionem: in perpetuum utemini opera, eorum: fratribus autem vestris filiis Israel quisque fratri suo non dominabitur dure.
47. And if a sojourner or stranger wax rich by thee, and thy brother that dwelleth by him wax poor, and sell himself unto the stranger or sojourner by thee, or to the stock of the stranger’s family:
47. Si autem apprehenderint manus peregrini et advenae qui est apud te, et attenuatus fuerit frater tuus qui apud illum versatur, seque vendiderit peregrino et advenae qui est apud te, vel stirpi familiae peregrini:
48. After that he is sold he may be redeemed again; one of his brethren may redeem him:
48. Postquam vendiderit se, redemptio erit ei: unus e fratribus ejus redimet eum:
49. Either his uncle, or his uncle’s son, may redeem him, or any that is nigh of kin unto him of his family may redeem him; or, if he be able, he may redeem himself.

50. And he shall reckon with him that bought him, from the year that he was sold to him, unto the year of jubilee: and the price of his sale shall be according unto the number of years, according to the time of an hired servant shall it be with him.
50. Et supputabit cum eo qui emit ipsum, ab anno quo se vendidit illi, usque ad annum Jubilaei, aestimabiturque pecunia venditionis ejus secundum numerum annorum: et secundum dies mercenarii fiet cum eo.
51. If there be yet many years behind, according unto them he shall give again the price of his redemption out of the money that he was bought for.
51. Si adhuc multi fuerint anni, secundum eos restituet redemptionem suam de argento venditionis suae.
52. And if there remain but few years unto the year of jubilee, then he shall count with him, and according unto his years shall he give him again the price of his redemption.
52. Quod si parum reliquum sit ex annis usque ad annum Jubilaei, tunc supputabit cum eo: et secundum annos suos restituet redemptionem suam.
53. And as a yearly hired servant shall he be with him: and the other shall not rule with rigor over him in thy sight.
53. Tanquam mercenarius annuus erit cum illo: non dominabitur ei dure in oculis tuis.
54. And if he be not redeemed in these years, then he shall go out in the year of jubilee, both he, and his children with him.
54. Si non se redemerit in illis, egredietur in anno Jubilaei ipse et filii ejus:
55. For unto me the children of Israel are servants; they are my servants, whom I brought forth out of the land of Egypt: I am the Lord your God.
55. Quia mihi sunt filii Israel servi, servi mei sunt quos eduxi e terra AEgypti: ego Jehova Deus vester.

19. All the firstling males. Another caution is added, that they should make no profit of the first-born; for they might have used the labor of the ox in plowing, or as a beast of burden; they might also have sheared the lambs, and have afterwards brought a deteriorated animal into the tabernacle. God commands, therefore, that what was due to Him should be honestly and absolutely paid. But, if good laws sprang from evil habits, it hence appears with what audacious greediness men have ever been led away to wicked gains, since it was necessary that they should be prohibited by an express edict from seeking to enrich themselves at God’s expense. Wherefore, it is not to be wondered at that men are acute and sagacious in cheating each other, since they by no means hesitate to deceive God by wicked artifices.
